title: ECB Policy Rates
content:
ECB at a Glance

  • Established in 1998, the ECB is the monetary authority of the Eurozone.
  • Its mandate centres on price stability (2% inflation target).
  • Since October 2008, the ECB has shifted from a scarce-reserve corridor to a floor system.
  • Its policy stance is transmitted through three rates: DF, MRO, and MLF.

Historical Cycles

[CHART1]

1. 1999-2000 – First tightening after euro launch

ECB hikes from 2.5% to 4.75% as euro-area growth accelerates, oil prices surge, money/credit grow fast and the euro is weak. Goal: establish anti-inflation credibility and contain medium-term inflation risks.

2. 2001-2003 – Dot-com bust and cautious cuts

ECB cuts from 4.75% to 2% as dot-com crash, global slowdown and 9/11 hit demand. Moves slower than the Fed because headline inflation is still pushed up by oil/tax effects.

3. 2003-2005 – Low and flat “Goldilocks”

Main refi held at 2%. Growth moderate, inflation near 2%, no acute financial stress. ECB sees this as a suitably accommodative, stable stance.

4. 2005-2007 – Pre-crisis normalisation

ECB hikes from 2% to 4% as growth is strong, oil and commodities rise, credit and money expand, and inflation runs above target. Aim: prevent overheating and de-anchoring of inflation expectations.

5. 2008-2009 – Global Financial Crisis

After a last hike to 4.25% in July 2008, ECB slashes to 1% after Lehman and deep recession. Launches full-allotment LTROs and bond purchases to stabilise banks, credit and inflation.

6. 2010-2011 – Sovereign crisis and policy mistake

ECB raises rates twice to 1.5% in 2011 on above-target inflation, while sovereign crisis in periphery explodes (Greece, Ireland, Portugal, then Italy and Spain later); partially offsets via SMP bond buying. Quickly reverses hikes as crisis worsens – widely judged a mistake.

7. 2012-2014 – Draghi, OMT, forward guidance, NIRP

“Whatever it takes” and OMT backstop sovereigns and reduce fragmentation. ECB cuts rates to ~0, introduces forward guidance, then NIRP and targeted LTROs to fight recession and deflation risk.

8. 2015-2018 – QE and prolonged ultra-easy policy

ECB runs large-scale APP (QE), keeps main refi at 0 and depo down to –0.40%, plus TLTROs. Growth improves but inflation is still weak, so net purchases only stop at end-2018; rates remain at the lower bound.

9. 2019-2021 – Renewed easing + COVID shock

2019: depo cut to –0.50%, QE restarted, stronger forward guidance and reserve tiering as inflation undershoots. 2020–21: COVID recession → PEPP and massive TLTROs while keeping rates at 0 / –0.50% to prevent financial and deflationary spiral.

10. 2022-2023 – Fastest hiking cycle

Post-COVID + energy shock push inflation into double digits. ECB ends net purchases and hikes from –0.50% to 4% on the depo rate (July 2022–Sept 2023) to re-anchor inflation expectations despite weak growth.

11. From 2024 – Disinflation and cautious easing

Inflation falls back towards target and growth is soft. From June 2024, ECB starts cutting from very restrictive levels and signals a gradual, data-dependent easing path to avoid over-tightening.

title: Fed Policy Rates
content:
Fed at a Glance

  • Established in 1913, the Fed is the central bank of the United States.
  • Its dual mandate targets price stability (2% inflation goal) and maximum employment.
  • Since October 2008, the Fed has shifted from a scarce-reserve corridor to a floor system.
  • The Fed steers overnight rates through two administered tools: IORB and ON RRP.
  • Other relevant rates: FFTR (FFTRL–FFTRU) and DPCREDIT.

Historical Cycles

[CHART1]

1. 1999–2000 – Pre-dot-com tightening

Fed hikes from 4.75% to 6.5% as growth booms, labor markets tighten, and inflation risks rise. Aim: preempt overheating and asset bubbles.

2. 2001–2003 – Post-crash easing

Cuts from 6.5% to 1% after dot-com bust, 2001 recession, and 9/11. Inflation slows, unemployment rises. Introduces early forward guidance; flags deflation risk.

3. 2004–2006 – Normalization in housing boom

Raises rates steadily from 1% to 5.25% in 17 steps as credit and housing surge. Goal: withdraw stimulus and anchor expectations.

4. 2007–2008 – Crisis and ZIRP

Cuts rapidly from 5.25% to 0–0.25% amid subprime meltdown and systemic collapse. Launches QE, emergency lending, and interest on reserves.

5. 2009–2015 – ZIRP, QE, and guidance

Keeps rates at 0–0.25% for 7 years. Runs QE1–3, sharpens forward guidance, and transitions to floor system using IOER and ON RRP.

6. 2015–2018 – Liftoff and runoff

Liftoff in Dec 2015 as labor market tightens and inflation approaches 2%. Starts runoff. Controls rates via IOER and ON RRP.

7. 2019 – Insurance cuts and repo stress

Cuts 3 times to 1.5% amid trade tensions and weak inflation. Repo market dislocations prompt renewed liquidity injections.

8. 2020–2021 – COVID shock and QE infinity

Returns to 0–0.25%, launches unlimited QE and broad credit backstops. Shifts to outcome-based guidance and adopts FAIT.

9. 2022–2023 – Inflation fight

Hikes from 0.25% to 5.5% in record time as inflation spikes. Ends QE, begins QT, and prioritizes price stability.

10. 2024–2025 – Disinflation and recalibration

With inflation easing, Fed cuts cautiously from mid-2024. By late 2025, rates fall to 3.75–4.00%. Easing remains gradual and conditional.

title: Key Global Policy Rates
content:
Reading Notes

  • Focus on 9 key central banks only: Fed, ECB, BoJ, BoE, PBoC, SNB, BoC, RBA, Norges.
  • ON MM rates are used as policy rate proxies.

ON MM Rate Profiles

[CHART1]

➤ Structurally low and stable SW/JP

  • JP has fought deflation for decades, from the post-bubble collapse (1990s) and weak demographics.
  • SW has fought the strong-CHF problem for decades, caused by persistent current-account surpluses, safe-haven inflows, and lower inflation than peers.

➤ Unsynchronized and oscillating CN

  • CN runs scarce-reserve corridor to actively manage domestic liquidity and credit, because QE-style excess reserves would amplify leverage and bubble risks in China’s bank-dominated, real-estate-dependent system, unlike DM floor where deeper capital markets can better absorb such risks.

[CHART2]

➤ Clear upward slope

    • Higher-rate regimes exhibit higher realized volatility.

    ➤ DM cluster vs CN/JP outliers

    • Most rates are mutually correlated except CN/JP, reflecting their idiosyncratic regimes.

    [CHART3]

    ➤ Post-2008 DM regime shifts

    • Most DM CBs shift from scarce-reserve corridor to abundant-reserve floor, visible in the collapse of ON MM rate volatility.

    ➤ Alternative regimes (JP/CN)

    • JP: ZIRP/NIRP + YCC, maintaining rates at or near 0% and long-term yields capped by fixed-rate BoJ operations.
    • CN: Volatile scarce-reserve corridor, where overnight spikes reflect intentional and frequent liquidity fine-tuning by the PBoC.

    Historical Cycles

    [CHART4]
    5-day moving average of ON MM rates across countries.

    1. 1999–2000 — HIKING Late-cycle tech boom

    Strong US growth + asset bubble → broad DM tightening.

    2. 2001–2003 — EASING Dotcom + 9/11 recession

    Demand slumps → coordinated DM rate cuts.

    3. 2004–2007 — HIKING Housing / credit / commodity boom

    Overheating + rising inflation → synchronized tightening.

    4. 2008–2009 — EASING GFC

    Systemic collapse → emergency cuts to zero + QE.

    5. 2010–2011 — HIKING Temporary commodity inflation

    Oil shock (>$100) → short, failed tightening attempt.

    6. 2012–2015 — EASING Euro crisis + deflation risk

    ZLB for G3 → forward guidance, QE, and other balance-sheet tools.

    7. 2016–2019 — HIKING US-led, mild global tightening

    Fed normalises; others stay dovish → partial divergence.

    8. 2020–2021 — EASING COVID crisis

    Fastest synchronized DM rate cuts in modern history + QE.

    9. 2022–2023 — HIKING Inflation shock

    Strongest tightening since the 1970s.

    10. 2024–Now — EASING Disinflation

    Inflation moderates; growth softens → DM tilt back toward cuts.


    [CHART5]
    $$\text{Hybrid MAD} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} |x_i - \text{median}(x)| \quad \text{where } x_i \text{ are ON MM rates across countries.}$$

    🔵 Convergence

    1. 2001 – Dotcom Bust → coordinated easing.
    2. 2009–2010 – GFC → universal zero-rate policy.
    3. 2020–2022 – COVID → synchronized emergency cuts.

    🔴 Divergence

    1. 2002 – Fed kept cutting post-9/11; ECB stayed cautious.
    2. Late 2008 – US crisis hit first, Fed cut fast; ECB lagged, focused on inflation
    3. 2011 – ECB hiked prematurely (mistakenly); others held or eased.
    4. 2023–Now – Inflation hit unevenly, it’s the stacking of multiple asymmetric shocks (energy, trade, fiscal, labor, housing).

    Mechanics of Policy Rate Transmission

    ➝ Price of Credit Channel

    Policy rate ↓ → money-market rates ↓ → banks’ funding costs ↓ → lending rates ↓ → price of credit ↓ → demand for credit ↑ → borrowing ↑ → consumption ↑, investment ↑

    ➝ Credit-Supply Channel

    Policy rate ↓ → money-market rates ↓ → banks’ funding costs ↓ → banks’ willingness to lend ↑ → credit supply ↑ → consumption ↑, investment ↑

    ➝ Returns-On-Savings Channel

    Policy rate ↓ → money-market rates ↓ → yield on savings accounts ↓ → consumption ↑, investment ↑

    ➝ Asset-Price Channel

    Policy rate ↓ → money-market rates ↓ → risk-free rate ↓ → discount rate ↓ → present value of cash flows ↑ → asset valuations ↑ → bonds ↑ (yields ↓), equities ↑, and real estate ↑ →

    • wealth ↑ → consumption ↑
    • cost of capital ↓ → investment ↑
    • collateral values ↑ → leverage capacity ↑ → credit ↑
    • borrower net worth ↑ → credit risk ↓ → credit availability ↑ → credit ↑

    ➝ Exchange-Rate Channel

    Policy rate ↓ → capital inflows ↓, capital outflows ↑ → currency depreciation → exports ↑, import prices ↑ (imported inflation ↑)

    ➝ Expectations Channel

    Policy rate ↓ + dovish communication → change expectations about future short rates, inflation, and economic conditions →

    • bonds ↑ → long-term yields ↓
    • risky assets ↑ → equities ↑, real estate ↑
    • borrowing ↑ → credit demand & supply ↑
    • consumption ↑, investment ↑
